newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Maine company hopes to revive flax.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Maine company hopes to revive flax.

text.p: Timothy Neidermann looks at the fields of northern Maine and dreams of reviving a textile industry laid low in the United States by the economics of slavery.
Neidermann believes this rural area where summer arrives late and leaves early has the ideal growing climate for flax -- the wheat-like plant whose sturdy fibers are spun to make linen.
"Linen's cool. When you come down to it, that's what drives us. We think the stuff's cool and we want everyone to think so," laughs Neidermann, a co-founder of the U.S. Flax and Linen Co.

Five years after the company planted its first crop, the idea of reviving a flax and linen industry in the United States is gaining political and financial support -- enough for the company to double its planned acreage for this year.

The first blankets to be woven in the United States from the Maine flax are coming off the looms of a small mill in Hallowell, and a textile conglomerate, Interface Inc., has invested in next year's crop.

Flax was widely grown in the northeastern United States in the 18th and early 19th centuries. It was considered so important that Maine once required all farmers to plant at least a small crop every year.

Despite that effort, flax could not compete with cotton that was produced less expensively with slave labour on southern plantations. Eli Whitney's invention of the cotton gin in 1794 sealed flax's fate.
"(From then) all of the manufacturing effort was taken forward by cotton," said Noel Mount, whose Brahms-Mount Textile Inc. mill is weaving the first linen blankets from Maine-grown flax.
Flax is still grown in the Northern Plains region of the United States. But those plants have been bred to produce linseed oil cigarette paper and do not have the fibers needed to make quality linen.
Flax is grown for textile production in several countries around the world, but farms in France and Belgium are generally regarded as producing the best quality.
"No one has been able to equal (the Europeans') quality until now," boasts Niedermann, who said the key was finding a climate that would allow the plants to grow at a slow, steady pace.

"What we discovered about the Aroostook County climate is even though it can get quite hot in the summertime, on average it's cool," said Neidermann. "It cools down at night ... you have a cold spring."
Reintroducing the crop has proven challenging. The specialised harvesting equipment designed for the flat fields of Normandy often breaks down on the hills and rocky soil of northern Maine.

"All the (farming) information we have now is European information, and most of it we can throw out the window and start over again. Everything is so totally different," said Ed Hastillo, Neidermann's partner.

Interface, which is switching to the use of all natural fibers, was also forced to go overseas for technology -- purchasing the equipment of a defunct Northern Ireland linen spinning mill and moving it to New England.

While Interface, a carpet and interior fabrics producer, is attracted by the flax fiber's durability, Brahams-Mount Textile believes upscale domestic consumers who now buy European linen will be drawn to an entirely U.S.-made product.

"The niche market at the top of the pile, they know linen today ... and they buy linen today like they did a hundred years ago. They look for it," said Mount, who has spent three decades in the textile industry.

Maine officials have identified flax as one of the state's top economic development priorities, and they hope it can boost the economy of a region of the state that has been losing jobs and population.
The U.S. Flax and Linen Co. expects to contract farmers to plant 2,000 acres in 1997, and Neiderman believes there will eventually be enough demand for Maine to grow more than 20,000 acres annually.
